reason: Inverting this would make update reject valid arguments or accept --bootstrap.
Removing this would let `update --bootstrap` run instead of being reported as an unknown argument.
Inverting this would refuse runs that have a terminal and allow runs that have none.
With no home directory, the run would no longer exit with code 1.
The restarted program would start as the wrong command, for example setup.
Without this, end of input would loop forever or count as yes.
Checking for an install record first could break the restarted run's resume.
An update would be attempted even when mmhmem is not set up.
The not-set-up case would no longer exit early with its exit code.
An unknown newest release would be reported as up to date with exit 0 instead of exit 1.
A failed lookup would no longer return exit code 1.
Inverting this would update when the user declines.
Swapping this with the refusal check would change which result is reported first: cancel or refused.
Declining would no longer exit with the cancelled code.
With no trusted key, the update would go ahead instead of being refused with exit 1.
The failure reason would be omitted, or shown for other notes.
Unexpected flow states would no longer fail with exit 1.
The bootstrap path would install against the user's answer.
A declined bootstrap would no longer return the cancelled code.
The user would be asked when nothing changes, or changes would be applied without asking.
The 'updated' line would be shown on the wrong path.
Changes would be applied after the user said no.
Declining the changes would still apply them, or return the wrong code.
The problems heading would be shown when there are no problems, or hidden when there are.
'Done' would be printed despite failures or pending steps, or left out when everything succeeded.
It only computes result lines from the flow, so it is a pure formatting function.
